source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Treat the presentation as uncomplicated dyspepsia without further evaluation, even though a positive Murphy sign raises concern for gallbladder inflammation.","B":"Diagnose acute cholecystitis from symptoms alone and omit imaging, because laboratory testing and imaging cannot improve diagnostic confidence.","C":"Suspect acute cholecystitis and obtain right-upper-quadrant ultrasound as the usual initial imaging study to evaluate the gallbladder and biliary tract.","D":"Use colonoscopy as the first imaging procedure because right-upper-quadrant pain with a Murphy sign primarily indicates colonic rather than biliary disease."}}
source_row.rationale: Right upper-quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and a positive Murphy sign are compatible with acute cholecystitis. Ultrasound is generally the initial imaging test used to evaluate suspected acute cholecystitis and gallstones; diagnosis incorporates clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings.
source_row.source_detail: WSES 2020 guideline Section 1, Statements 1.1–1.3: do not rely on one feature; use combined history/exam/labs/imaging; RUQ pain, fever and Murphy sign are useful features; ultrasound is preferred initial imaging. World J Emerg Surg 2020;15:61, DOI 10.1186/s13017-020-00336-x; currentness reviewed 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client has right upper-quadrant pain, fever, nausea, and a positive Murphy sign. Which diagnostic approach is most appropriate?
